'''Richard Allan Ferrell''' (1926–2005) was an American [[theoretical physicist]], specializing in condensed matter physics and statistical physics.<ref name=ObitPT>{{cite journal|title=Obituary of Richard Alan Ferrell|author=Sucher, Joseph|author2=Scalapino, Douglas|author3=Prange, Richard|date=18 May 2006|doi=10.1063/PT.4.2323|journal=Physics Today|issue=5 |page=18036 |bibcode=2006PhT..2006e8036. |url=https://physicstoday.scitation.org/do/10.1063/pt.4.2323/full/|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

==Biography==
Richard A. Ferrell grew up in [[Orange County, California]]. During WW II he served in the U. S. Navy.<ref name=ObitUMd>{{cite web|author=Prange, Richard|author2=Sucher, Joseph|author3=Scalapino, Douglas|title=Richard A. Ferrell (1926–2005)|website=Department of Physics, University of Maryland|url=https://umdphysics.umd.edu/about-us/2-uncategorised/539-richard-a-ferrell-.html}} (This obituary misspells Ferrell middle name as "Alan" — instead of the correct "Allan". The problems in "Smythe" mentioned in the obituary refer to [[William Smythe (physicist)|William R. Smythe]]'s textbook ''Static and Dynamic Electricity''.)</ref> His mother, Elsie Hopper Ferrell (1906–1995), graduated in 1949 with an M.D. from the [[David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA|University of California, Los Angeles School of Medicine]].<ref>{{cite book|chapter=The Degree of Doctor of Medicine|title=University of California, the Eighty-sixth Commencement|date=June 1949|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vgE5AQAAMAAJ&pg=PA166}}</ref> He graduated from the [[California Institute of Technology]] with a B.S. in 1948<ref>{{cite web|title=California Institute of Technology, Commencement Exercises|website=caltech.edu|date=June 11, 1948|page=4|url=https://campuspubs.library.caltech.edu/2502/1/June_11%2C_1948.pdf}}</ref> and an M.S. in 1949.<ref>{{cite web|title=California Institute of Technology, Commencement Exercises|website=caltech.edu|date=June 10, 1949|page=6|url=https://campuspubs.library.caltech.edu/2496/1/June_10%2C_1949.pdf}}</ref> He matriculated in 1949 at [[Princeton University]] as a graduate student with fellowship granted by the Atomic Energy Commission and in 1951 won the $1000 top prize in an essay contest sponsored by the [[Gravity Research Foundation]].<ref>{{cite journal|title=Personals (Caltech alumni information)|journal=Engineering and Science|date=January 1951|volume=14|issue=4|page=24|publisher=California Institute of Technology|url=https://calteches.library.caltech.edu/129/2/ES14.4.1951.pdf}}</ref> He married Miriam Laura Conover in 1951.<ref>{{cite news|title=Marriages|newspaper=Princeton Herald|volume=28|issue=98|date=October 10, 1951}}</ref> In 1952 he received his Ph.D. from Princeton University.<ref>{{cite web|title=Richard Allan Ferrell, Ph.D.|website=Physics Tree|url=https://academictree.org/physics/peopleinfo.php?pid=71270}}</ref> As a postdoc he spent the academic year 1952–1953 under the supervision of [[Werner Heisenberg]] at the [[Max Planck Institute for Physics]] (which at that time was located in [[Göttingen]]). At the invitation of [[John S. Toll]], Ferrell joined in 1953 the faculty of the [[University of Maryland]], where he was promoted to full professor in 1959<ref name=ObitUMd/> and retired as professor emeritus in 1993. He was the author or co-author of more than 150 scientific articles and could write in French, German, and Russian.<ref name=ObitWP>{{cite news|title=Obituary. U-Md. Prof. Richard Ferrell|date=December 12, 2005|newspaper=Washington Post|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/2005/12/12/u-md-prof-richard-ferrell/5867787f-23fb-4d56-8887-cb9591ae7076/}}</ref> His 1960 article ''Electron-nucleus hyperfine interactions in atoms'' was mentioned in Robert H. Romer's list of memorable papers published in the ''[[American Journal of Physics]]'' from the years 1933 to 1990.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Editorial: Memorable papers from the ''American Journal of Physics'', 1933 to 1990|journal=American Journal of Physics|date=March 1991|volume=59|issue=3|pages=201–207|doi=10.1119/1.16562 |url=https://www.aapt.org/Publications/ajp-themepdfsandpurcell/MemorablePapers.pdf|last1=Romer |first1=Robert H. |bibcode=1991AmJPh..59..201R }}</ref> His sabbatical leaves included visiting positions at the [[CERN]] laboratory<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Glaser |first1=V. |last2=Ferrell |first2=R. A. |date=1961-02-01 |title=Lifetime of the Neutral Pion |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRev.121.886 |journal=Physical Review |language=en |volume=121 |issue=3 |pages=886–892 |doi=10.1103/PhysRev.121.886 |bibcode=1961PhRv..121..886G |issn=0031-899X|url-access=subscription }}</ref> in Geneva and the [[Max Planck Society#Max Planck Institutes|Max Planck Institutes]] in Munich and Stuttgart.<ref name=ObitWP/>

In May 1976 Ferrell with several American colleagues attended a Soviet-American physics symposium and also attended the Sunday Seminar of [[Mark Azbel]] and other [[refusenik]]s. After returning to the United States, Ferrell and his colleagues published a letter of support for the refuseniks.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1063/1.3023301|title=Sunday in Moscow|year=1976|last1=Cummings|first1=Herman Z.|last2=Pershan|first2=Peter S.|last3=Klein|first3=Miles V.|last4=Platzman|first4=P. M.|last5=Varma|first5=C. M.|last6=Falicov|first6=L. M.|last7=Bendow|first7=Bernard|last8=Ferrell|first8=Richard A.|last9=Stephen|first9=M. J.|journal=Physics Today|volume=29|issue=2|pages=9–11|bibcode=1976PhT....29R...9C }}</ref>

He not only planted trees in University Park, Maryland, but also helped to persuade officials to have trees planted along [[U.S. Route 1]] in [[College Park, Maryland]] and on the campus of the University of Maryland. Upon his death he was survived by his widow, a daughter, a son, and three grandchildren.<ref name=ObitWP/>

In 2001 the University of Maryland established the Richard A. Ferrell Distinguished Faculty Fellowship.<ref>{{cite web|title=Richard A. Ferrell Distinguished Faculty Fellowship Fund|website=Giving to Maryland, University of Maryland|url=https://giving.umd.edu/Giving/Fund.php?name=richard-a-ferrell-distinguished-faculty-fellowship-fund}}</ref>

==Ferrell–Glover–Tinkham sum rule==
The Ferrell–Glover–Tinkham sum rule<ref>{{cite journal|author=Ferrell, R. A.|author2=Glover III, Rolfe E.|date=February 1958|title=Conductivity of superconducting films: A sum rule|journal=Physical Review|volume=109|issue=4|pages=1398–1399|doi=10.1103/PhysRev.109.1398|bibcode=1958PhRv..109.1398F }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author=Tinkham, Michael|author2=Ferrell, R. A.|date=April 1959|title=Determination of the superconducting skin depth from the energy gap and sum rule|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=2|issue=8|pages=331–333|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.2.331|bibcode=1959PhRvL...2..331T }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author=Homes, C. C.|author2=Dordevic, S. V.|author3=Bonn, D. A.|author4=Liang, R.|author5=Hardy, W. N.|year=2004|title=Sum rules and energy scales in the high-temperature superconductor YBa<sub>2</sub>Cu<sub>3</sub>O<sub>6+''x''</sub>|journal=Physical Review B|volume=69|issue=2|article-number=024514|doi= 10.1103/PhysRevB.69.024514|arxiv=cond-mat/0303506 |bibcode=2004PhRvB..69b4514H |s2cid=119390570 }} [https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0303506 arXiv preprint]</ref> "asserts that the finite frequency response which is lost in the superconducting transition reappears at the zero frequency 'superconductivity' delta-function."<ref name=ObitUMd/> The sum rule is important for many [[High-temperature superconductivity|high-''T''<sub>c</sub> superconductivity]] analyses.<ref name=ObitPT/>

As postdocs in 1956, [[Michael Tinkham]] and Rolf Eldridge Glover III<ref>{{cite journal|title=Obituary. Rolfe Eldridge Glover III|author=Ferrell, Richard A.|author2=Lobb, Christopher J. Lobb|author3=Tinkham, Michael|journal=Physics Today|volume=58|issue=3|pages=90–91|date=March 2005|doi=10.1063/1.1897575|doi-access=free}}</ref> demonstrated<ref>{{cite journal|title=Transmission of Superconducting Films at Millimeter-Microwave and Far Infrared Frequencies|author=Glover III, R. E. Glover|author2=Tinkham, M.|journal=Phys. Rev.|volume=104|issue=3|pages=844–845|date=November 1956|doi=10.1103/PhysRev.104.844|bibcode=1956PhRv..104..844G }}</ref> "the existence of a superconducting "energy gap" by showing that light below a certain frequency was transmitted much more readily through a superconducting film than through a normal metal film. This counter-intuitive result was a landmark confirmation of the famous [[BCS theory|Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer theory of superconductivity]]."<ref>{{cite book|last1=Clarke|first1=John|author-link=John Clarke (physicist)|author2=Silvera, Isaac F.|author3=Beasley, Malcolm R.|title=Michael Tinkham, 1928-2010 (Biographical Memoirs)|date=2015|publisher=National Academy of Sciences|page=1|url=https://www.nasonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/tinkham-michael.pdf}} (See also pages 5 & 6.)</ref> Subsequently, Glover and Tinkham collaborated with Ferrell on the theory of their discovery.
